title: Plants of Bangladesh: Diversity and Adaptation

questions.stem: Sort these living things into flowering plants, non-flowering plants and things that are not plants.
questions.explanation: Flowering plants make flowers and seeds. Ferns and mosses make spores and pine trees make seeds in cones. Mushrooms and moulds are fungi, not plants.

questions.stem: Match each plant to its adaptation.
pairs: breathing roots that stick up out of salty mud
thick stem that stores water, and spines instead of leaves
waxy leaves that water rolls off
bendy trunk that does not snap in storms
questions.explanation: Each adaptation suits the plant's habitat: air roots for muddy ground, floats for water, a water store for deserts, waxy leaves for wet places and a bendy trunk for storms.

questions.stem: Rice plants do not have flowers.
questions.explanation: Rice is a flowering plant. Its flowers are small and green, so we often do not notice them. The grains of rice are its seeds.

questions.stem: Ferns and mosses do not grow from seeds. They grow from tiny ___.
questions.explanation: Ferns and mosses are non-flowering plants. They make tiny cells called spores that can grow into new plants.

questions.stem: A pine tree makes its seeds inside cones, not flowers. What kind of plant is it?
options: a flowering plant
a fungus
a non-flowering plant
an animal
questions.explanation: Pine trees are conifers, which are non-flowering plants. They still make seeds, but inside cones.

questions.stem: Mushrooms are not plants. They belong to a different group called…
options: fungi
mosses
ferns
conifers
questions.explanation: Mushrooms and moulds are fungi. They cannot make their own food from sunlight, which plants can.

questions.stem: Why do many mangrove trees have roots that poke up out of the mud?
options: to catch fish for the tree to eat
to drink salty water from above
to hold up the flowers
to take in air, because the wet salty mud has very little air
questions.explanation: Roots need air too. The salty mud of the Sundarbans has very little air, so breathing roots grow up into the air.

questions.stem: Tisha says, 'A cactus would grow well in the Sundarbans.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.model_answer: No. A cactus is adapted to dry places. In the wet, salty, muddy Sundarbans its roots would rot and it could not survive.
questions.explanation: Adaptations only help in the right habitat. A cactus stores water for dry places, but the Sundarbans is wet and salty, so it would not survive there.

questions.stem: Put these steps in order to show how a storm can harm a rice field near the coast.
sequence: A strong cyclone pushes sea water over the land.
Salty water floods a rice field.
The salt stops the rice roots from taking in water.
The rice grows badly or dies.
questions.explanation: Rice is not adapted to salt. Salty water pushed inland by a storm surge can kill crops, so natural changes can change which plants can grow in a place.

questions.stem: Water hyacinth floats because its leaf stalks are swollen and full of ___.
questions.explanation: The spongy, air-filled stalks work like floats, so the plant stays on the surface while its roots hang down to take in minerals from the water.

questions.stem: Which are adaptations of mangrove trees? Choose all that are right.
options: breathing roots that take in air
prop roots that hold the tree steady in soft mud
leaves that can get rid of extra salt
a thick stem that stores water
spongy stalks that make the plant float
questions.explanation: Mangroves live in salty, soft, airless mud. A thick water-storing stem belongs to a cactus and floating stalks belong to water hyacinth.

questions.stem: Water hyacinth is a problem and a gift. Sort these effects.
questions.explanation: Water hyacinth covers ponds and canals, which causes problems. But farmers and craft workers have found clever uses for it, such as floating gardens (dhap) and woven baskets.

questions.stem: The lotus has long, hollow stems. What is their job?
options: to store water for dry weather
to carry air down to its roots in the mud
to make the plant sink
to hold up the roots like props
questions.explanation: The roots of a lotus are buried in muddy water with little air. The hollow stems carry air down to them.

questions.stem: Look at the mangrove tree. Which labelled part holds the tree steady in the soft mud?
questions.image_alt: A mangrove tree with breathing roots and prop roots in salty mud, labelled breathing roots, prop roots, salty mud and salty water.
options: prop roots
salty mud
breathing roots
salty water
questions.explanation: Prop roots spread out like legs and hold the tree firmly in the soft mud, so storms and tides do not knock it over. The breathing roots take in air.

questions.stem: Which of these is **not** a plant?
questions.explanation: A mushroom is a fungus. It cannot make its own food from sunlight, so it is not a plant.

questions.stem: Match each plant to the adaptation that helps it survive.
pairs: waxy leaves that water rolls off
questions.explanation: Water slides off a lotus leaf, a cactus keeps a store of water in its stem for dry weather, and a palm bends in the wind instead of snapping.

questions.stem: Which of these are flowering plants? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Sunflowers, lotuses and roses all grow flowers that make seeds. A mushroom is a fungus, so it is not a plant at all.

questions.stem: Where is each plant adapted to live? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: A cactus stores water for deserts, lotus and rice grow in water or flooded fields, and palm trees bend in the strong winds of the coast.

questions.stem: Which plant has waxy leaves that water rolls off and long hollow stems that carry air down to its roots in the mud?
questions.explanation: The lotus lives in muddy pools. Its waxy leaves shed water and its hollow stems bring air to the roots.

questions.stem: A cyclone floods a farm near Khulna with salty sea water. The farmer wants to grow a crop that has a chance of surviving next season. What is the sensible choice?
options: the same ordinary rice, but with more salty water
a cactus, because it stores water
lotus, because it likes standing water
a variety of rice that can grow in slightly salty soil
questions.explanation: Salt-tolerant rice is bred to cope with salty soil. Ordinary rice is not adapted to salt, and a cactus is adapted to dry places, not salty ones.

questions.stem: Mina finds green moss on a damp, shady garden wall. Where else would she be most likely to find moss?
options: on a damp, shady tree trunk
on a hot, dry, sunny road
on a tin roof in the sun
in dry sand
questions.explanation: Mosses are non-flowering plants that grow in damp, shady places, where their spores can grow and they do not dry out.

questions.stem: A village pond is covered by water hyacinth and the fishing boats are stuck. What is a sensible way to use the plants once they are pulled out?
options: pour strong chemicals into the pond
put them back in the pond to rot
pile them up for compost or a floating vegetable garden
burn them on the pond bank all week
questions.explanation: In Bangladesh people use water hyacinth for compost, cattle food, craft baskets and floating gardens (dhap). Chemicals would harm the fish and the water.

questions.stem: Raju sees green fuzzy mould growing on old bread. He says it is a small plant because it is green and it grows.
questions.explanation: Mould is a fungus, not a plant. It cannot make its own food from sunlight, so it gets its food by growing on the bread.

questions.stem: People in villages behind the Sundarbans say the forest protects them when a cyclone comes. Why?
options: The mangroves turn the cyclone away from the coast.
The mangroves stop the tide from coming in.
The mangroves make the rain stop.
The mangroves slow the wind and the waves.
questions.explanation: The trees and thick roots of the mangroves slow down the wind and the waves, so less force reaches the villages behind them.

questions.stem: A patch of water hyacinth covers 3 square metres of a pond and doubles its area every 2 weeks. How much will it cover after 6 weeks?
options: 9 square metres
24 square metres
18 square metres
12 square metres
questions.explanation: After 2 weeks: 6 m². After 4 weeks: 12 m². After 6 weeks: 24 m². 'Doubles' means multiply by 2 each time, not add 3.

questions.stem: Class 4B repeated the model-leaf test (example data). Plain leaves lost 10 g and 14 g of water. Waxy leaves lost 2 g and 4 g. On average, the plain leaves lost ___ times as much water as the waxy leaves.
questions.explanation: Mean for plain leaves = (10 + 14) ÷ 2 = 12 g. Mean for waxy leaves = (2 + 4) ÷ 2 = 3 g. 12 ÷ 3 = 4 times. A waxy coat stops a leaf losing so much water.

questions.stem: Class 4A tests whether a waxy coat stops model leaves (wet paper towels) drying out. Which choices would make the test **unfair**? Choose all that are right.
options: using a bigger paper towel for the waxy leaf
leaving the plain leaves in the shade and the waxy leaves in the sun
using the same amount of water on every leaf
weighing each leaf at the start and again after 3 hours
leaving the waxy leaves for 6 hours and the plain leaves for 3 hours
questions.explanation: Only the wax should change. Different sizes, different places and different times are extra changes. The same water and weighing at the start and end are good practice.

questions.stem: In a long drought, plant X has small waxy leaves and deep roots. Plant Y has large thin leaves and shallow roots. Which statement is best?
options: X survives better, because waxy leaves make water for the plant.
Y survives better, because large leaves can collect more rain.
Y survives better, because shallow roots are closer to the sun.
X survives better, because waxy leaves lose less water and deep roots reach water underground.
questions.explanation: Small waxy leaves lose little water to the air, and deep roots reach water below the dry surface. Plants do not make water, and large thin leaves lose more of it.

questions.stem: Joy says, 'Water hyacinth is only a problem. We should destroy all of it.' Give one reason why she may be right and one reason why she may be wrong.
questions.model_answer: She may be right because water hyacinth blocks boats, shades the water so fish get less light and air, and lets mosquitoes breed. She may be wrong because people use it for compost, floating gardens, cattle food and baskets.
questions.explanation: A good answer weighs both sides with evidence. Water hyacinth causes problems for boats, fish and health, but it is also a useful material for farmers and craft workers.

questions.stem: About a quarter of the Sundarbans was badly damaged by Cyclone Sidr in 2007, but the mangroves grew back over the following years. Hamid says, 'This proves that no kind of plant ever dies out after a cyclone.' Is Hamid's conclusion supported?
questions.explanation: The evidence only shows that the mangroves grew back. It does not tell us about every plant, and natural changes can make some plants die and new kinds take their place.
